item.text: {"text":"Recent research supports separating recency sensitivity from dependence on interaction order. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) proposes HRLI@K: whether the last observed item appears among recommendations. This measures last-item repetition, so it requires a separate diagnostic ranking when production recommendations exclude seen items. [Does It Look Sequential? (RecSys 2024)](https://github.com/Antondfger/Does-It-Look-Sequential) compares original and shuffled histories using HR@10, NDCG@10 and recommendation-set Jaccard overlap, finding weak sequential structure in several common datasets. [Petrov et al. (RecSys 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833) show that simple recency-weighted pairwise models outperform reproduced Transformer baselines on multiple benchmarks; strong ranking accuracy alone therefore does not establish higher-order sequence learning.\n\nSuggested diagnostic synthesis: freeze the trained model and compare final-position rankings after removing recent interactions, retaining only a recent suffix, and shuffling older interactions while preserving the last item. Compare targeted removals with repeated random removals matched for edit count; preserve item membership for shuffle controls. Report paired validation HR@10 changes, original top-item rank displacement and top-10 overlap, with variability across users and perturbation seeds. Separate deletion with sequence compaction from masking that preserves positions: they alter positional encoding and the final input differently. Stratify results by observable history length and repeated-item frequency; use title/description similarity only as an explicitly defined proxy for recurring interests. Greater recent-edit sensitivity than matched random-edit sensitivity supports reliance on recent context; resilience to older-order shuffling suggests weaker dependence on that ordering. These are model-behavior measurements, not causal evidence of user intent, conformity or diversity preferences."}
